issues.item: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile as a coherent pattern for a trauma-to-a-loved-one case: 'Cars hit by accident' suggests a specific road-traffic trauma cue, while 'Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place' implies separation/safety-context triggering. These could coexist, but without any supporting memory or appraisal content about separation, they look clinically mismatched within the trigger node.

issues.item: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory items describe vivid sensory re-experiencing of a frightening event, and the other appraisals emphasize unfairness and generalized vigilance, but nothing else suggests interpersonal betrayal. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one formulation, this appraisal would usually require supporting context (e.g. trusted person caused or enabled the harm), which is absent here.

The trigger profile is only weakly coherent with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one. 'Workplace' as a major trigger is hard to reconcile unless the loved-one trauma happened in the workplace or through occupational exposure, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. The other triggers (cars hit by accident, alcohol smell) imply a specific accident scene, making 'workplace' stand out as clinically questionable rather than part of the same trigger network.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Betrayal by someone I trusted' points toward an interpersonal trauma formulation, but the rest of the profile centers on sensory accident-related reminders and vivid perceptual memory. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this appraisal is difficult to integrate unless the loved one's trauma directly involved trusted-person betrayal, which is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: The Negative Appraisals node contains two items that are hard to reconcile with the trauma type and with each other. 'Constant Vigilance' implies an ongoing sense of current danger, but the formulation has no active Threat links and the rest of the profile is focused on accident-related reminders and vivid sensory memory rather than present threat. 'Self-Blame' is also difficult to fit with a loved-one accident trauma in this profile, because no other item suggests the patient had a causally responsible role in the event; combined with the injustice item, it creates a mixed appraisal pattern that lacks a clear coherent basis in the rest of the report.

issues.item: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: Within the Negative Appraisals node, strong endorsement of both injustice/external blame ('nothing has been done about it') and self-blame for causing the event pulls in opposing directions and is difficult to reconcile as the same dominant appraisal without additional context. For a trauma to a loved one, these two appraisals can coexist in milder form, but selected together as core items they suggest conflicting attribution styles within the same node.

vignette:
Leilani is a 71-year-old police officer who has served her small coastal community for over four decades. Married to her husband, Mako, for nearly fifty years, she had always taken pride in her ability to stay calm under pressure-until the night her son, Kaimana, died. He was twenty-eight, a new father, and had been at a friend's barbecue. Leilani had spoken to him on the phone that evening; she remembered telling him to be careful, that she would see him the next day. He said he loved her. Then he hung up. Thirty minutes later, she was dispatched to a single-vehicle crash on the coastal highway. When she arrived, the car was wrapped around a utility pole, and the smell of alcohol was thick in the air. She recognized the license plate. What she saw inside the wreckage-Kaimana's body, the blood, the stillness-has never left her. She tried to pull him out, but he was gone. The driver of the other vehicle, a man twice convicted for DUI, had walked away with minor injuries.

In the weeks that followed, Leilani could not stop replaying that night. The memories came not as stories but as vivid pictures: the twisted metal, the way her son's hand hung limp. Sometimes she heard things-the screech of tires, the thud of impact, her own voice calling his name-as if the sounds were trapped inside her skull. She had always believed that as a police officer she could protect people, especially her own family. Now she was certain that the event had happened because of the way she acted. She had not driven over to pick Kaimana up. She had not asked him to stay on the phone until he got home. She should have protected him, and she had failed. The thought that she could not stop bad things from happening-to anyone, ever again-began to feel like a permanent truth.

At work, the triggers were everywhere. Every time she saw a car that had been hit-even a minor fender bender in the station parking lot-her chest would tighten and she would see Kaimana's car. The smell of alcohol, whether from a suspect or a colleague's breath after a shift drink, made her stomach drop. She began to dread roll call, where accidents and DUI arrests were discussed. She stopped volunteering for traffic duty and started taking longer routes to avoid the stretch of highway where Kaimana died. At home, she refused to attend any gathering where beer or wine was served. Her husband tried to talk to her about what happened; she cut him off, saying she could not bear to hear the words "car accident" or "drunk driver." Over the months, she withdrew from her closest friends, stopped visiting her granddaughter, and spent her evenings sitting in the dark, replaying the images she could not control.

The consequences became unbearable. Her sergeant noticed she was avoiding critical assignments and urged her to take leave. Leilani refused. She told herself that if she stopped working, she would have no purpose left. But on duty she was hypervigilant, scanning every vehicle for signs of impact, flinching at any sudden sound. She began to believe that her helplessness was contagious-that if she stayed around her family, something bad would happen to them too. Her marriage grew strained; Mako said she was a ghost in the house. She knew he was right, but she could not explain what was happening inside her.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a minor incident that broke her composure. During a routine traffic stop, the driver had been drinking, and the smell hit her so hard that she doubled over and vomited behind her patrol car. Her partner, a young officer, looked at her with pity she could not bear. That night, she told Mako she needed to talk to someone. She is terrified that she will never feel safe again, and she is even more terrified that her family will see her as weak. But she is also hoping-faintly, cautiously-that maybe a stranger can help her carry the memory of that night without it crushing her every day.
